questions.question: How do you create a custom exception in Java?
questions.title: Creating Custom Exceptions in Java
questions.direct_answer: Extend **Exception** for a checked custom exception or **RuntimeException** for an unchecked one. Provide at least two constructors: one accepting a **message String** and one accepting a **message String plus a cause Throwable** for exception chaining.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can write a custom exception correctly from scratch
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a custom exception with no constructors, making it impossible to pass a message or cause
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why you provide multiple constructors and when to choose checked vs unchecked

sections.title: Custom Exception Template
Key Points
sections.content:
- Extend Exception for checked, RuntimeException for unchecked
- Always provide String message constructor
- Always provide String + Throwable cause constructor for exception chaining
- Name convention: ends with Exception (UserNotFoundException, ValidationException)
- Don't need to override any methods — super() delegates everything to Throwable
- Modern Java applications favor unchecked custom exceptions

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Creating a custom exception is straightforward — you extend either Exception or RuntimeException depending on whether you want it checked or unchecked. In modern Java development, you almost always extend RuntimeException. You need at least two constructors: one that takes a String message, and one that takes a String message plus a Throwable cause. The cause constructor is for exception chaining — when you catch a low-level exception and want to wrap it. You don't need to override any other methods because everything — getMessage(), getStackTrace(), getCause() — is inherited from Throwable.

beats.text: A custom exception is a class that extends either Exception (checked) or RuntimeException (unchecked). You write the class, provide constructors that call super(), and that's it. Everything else — getMessage, getCause, getStackTrace — is inherited from Throwable automatically.

Generic exceptions like RuntimeException tell callers nothing. UserNotFoundException or ValidationException communicate exactly what went wrong and let exception handlers respond precisely — 404 for not-found, 400 for validation failures.

items: Extend RuntimeException for unchecked (most common in modern Java) or Exception for checked
Message constructor — new UserNotFoundException(String message)
Cause constructor — new UserNotFoundException(String message, Throwable cause) — essential for exception chaining
Name ends with Exception by convention — UserNotFoundException, OrderValidationException

beats.text: candidates miss: You don't need to override any methods. Calling super(message) and super(message, cause) in your constructors is sufficient — Throwable provides getMessage(), getCause(), getStackTrace(), and printStackTrace() for free.

items: Providing only the message constructor — when you need to wrap a lower-level exception, you have no cause constructor to use.
Extending Exception when RuntimeException is appropriate — forces every caller to add try-catch or throws unnecessarily.

speakable_v2.cap: Extend RuntimeException, provide both constructors, follow the naming convention — that's a production-quality custom exception.

questions.question: When should you create a checked vs unchecked custom exception?
questions.title: Checked vs Unchecked Custom Exception Decision
questions.direct_answer: Create a **checked** custom exception when callers can meaningfully recover from the failure and you want the compiler to enforce handling. Create an **unchecked** exception for programming errors, configuration problems, or when propagating through many layers where requiring callers to handle it would be intrusive.

interviewer_intent.testing: Design judgment — not just knowing the syntax but knowing when to use each type
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always choosing checked because it 'forces handling' — without considering whether callers can recover
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that most modern frameworks (Spring, Hibernate) prefer unchecked and explain why

sections.title: When to Use Checked vs Unchecked Custom Exception
sections.content:
| Situation | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Caller can meaningfully recover | Checked |
| Programming/configuration error | Unchecked |
| Exception crosses multiple layers | Unchecked (avoids signature pollution) |
| External resource failure (file, network) | Checked |
| Validation error that caller must handle | Checked |
| Spring/JPA application layer exception | Unchecked |
| Systemic failure (DB down) | Unchecked |

sections.title: The Decision Framework
sections.content:
Ask yourself: **'Can the caller realistically handle this exception and recover?'**

- **FileUploadException** — the caller (web layer) can catch this and return a 400 error → Checked makes sense
- **ConfigurationException** — if configuration is wrong, the app can't start → Unchecked
- **UserNotFoundException** — the service calling the DAO can catch this and return 404 → Could be checked, but unchecked is cleaner

Most modern Java projects use unchecked custom exceptions for everything — they propagate to a global exception handler at the top.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The decision comes down to one question: can the caller meaningfully recover from this exception? If yes, checked makes sense — you're forcing them to think about the failure scenario. If no, unchecked is better — there's no point burdening every method in the call chain with it. In practice, most modern Java applications use unchecked custom exceptions for everything and rely on a global exception handler — like Spring's @ControllerAdvice — to translate exceptions into appropriate HTTP responses. This keeps method signatures clean and code readable. The Spring framework itself follows this approach — DataAccessException is unchecked.

questions.question: Why is it important to add a cause constructor to a custom exception?
questions.title: Why Custom Exceptions Need a Cause Constructor
questions.direct_answer: The cause constructor (`super(message, cause)`) enables **exception chaining** — preserving the original low-level exception that triggered yours. Without it, you lose the original stack trace, making production debugging much harder. It's a best practice to always provide the cause constructor.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical code quality awareness — do they know why the cause constructor matters
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating exceptions with only a String constructor, making chaining impossible
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a debugging scenario where the cause is critical to identifying the root issue

sections.title: With vs Without Cause Constructor
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The cause constructor is essential for debugging in production. Here's the scenario: your DAO catches a SQLException from the database and throws your custom DataException. If DataException only has a String constructor, you have to choose between losing the original SQLException or awkwardly stuffing the message into the string. If DataException has a cause constructor, you pass the SQLException as the cause — and now anyone who catches DataException can call getCause() to see the original database error with its full stack trace. Without this, a developer in production looking at logs sees 'DataException: query failed' but has no idea what the actual SQL problem was.

With cause constructor — getCause() returns the original exception; full stack trace preserved

Passing e.getMessage() as a string instead of the cause object — getMessage() is just text; the stack trace is gone.

speakable_v2.cap: Always provide the cause constructor — it's the difference between debugging in 5 minutes and debugging for 5 hours.

questions.question: How would you design exceptions for a layered Spring application?
questions.title: Exception Design in Spring Layered Architecture
questions.direct_answer: Create **layer-specific unchecked exceptions**: `DataAccessException` for the DAO layer, `ServiceException` for the service layer, and handle them in a **global exception handler** (`@ControllerAdvice`) in the web layer that maps exceptions to appropriate HTTP responses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Application design thinking — not just syntax but architecture
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a single generic exception everywhere, or letting SQLExceptions bubble up to the web layer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the ControllerAdvice pattern and explain how exceptions map to HTTP status codes

sections.title: Exception Design in Spring
sections.content:
A well-designed Spring application uses exception translation at each layer boundary:

1. **DAO layer** throws `DataAccessException extends RuntimeException` (Spring already provides this)
2. **Service layer** catches DAO exceptions and throws domain-specific exceptions:
   - `UserNotFoundException extends RuntimeException`
   - `ValidationException extends RuntimeException`
3. **Web layer** has `@ControllerAdvice` that catches domain exceptions and maps them to HTTP responses:
   - `UserNotFoundException` → 404
   - `ValidationException` → 400
   - Anything else → 500

sections.title: ControllerAdvice for Exception Mapping
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The pattern I use in Spring applications is to have layer-specific unchecked exceptions and a global handler at the top. The DAO layer throws DataAccessException — Spring actually provides this hierarchy already. The service layer throws domain-specific exceptions like UserNotFoundException or ValidationException, each extending RuntimeException. These propagate up freely without polluting method signatures. At the web layer, I use @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods that map each exception type to the right HTTP status code — 404 for UserNotFoundException, 400 for validation failures, 500 for anything unexpected. This keeps each layer clean and gives consistent, predictable API error responses.

questions.question: Should you add extra fields to a custom exception class?
questions.title: Extra Fields in Custom Exception Classes
questions.direct_answer: Yes, when they add diagnostic value. Adding fields like **error code**, **field name** (for validation errors), or **resource ID** (for not-found errors) lets exception handlers build more precise error responses without parsing the message string.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate thinks about exception usability from the handler's perspective
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Packing all context into the message string and then parsing it in handlers
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a ResourceNotFoundException with an id field and a ValidationException with a fieldName field

sections.title: Custom Exception with Extra Fields
Key Points
sections.content:
- Extra fields are useful when handlers need structured data beyond just the message
- Common extra fields: errorCode, fieldName (validation), resourceId, resourceType
- Avoid fields that make the exception too heavy or couple it to domain objects
- The exception handler can use these fields to build structured JSON error responses
- Don't add so many fields that the exception becomes a DTO — keep it focused

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Yes, extra fields can be very useful. The key question is: does the handler need this information to build a good error response? For example, with a ResourceNotFoundException, it's helpful to have the resource type and ID as separate fields. That way your ControllerAdvice can directly access resourceException.getResourceId() to put in the error response body, instead of parsing the exception message string. For validation exceptions, having a fieldName field tells the front end exactly which field failed. The rule of thumb is: add fields that exception handlers will actually use, not everything that might be related to the failure.

questions.question: What is serialVersionUID and why do exception classes often declare it?
questions.title: serialVersionUID in Exception Classes
questions.direct_answer: **serialVersionUID** is a unique identifier for serializable classes. Exception classes implement **Serializable** (inherited from Throwable), so Java warns if serialVersionUID is missing. You declare it to prevent `InvalidClassException` if the class changes between serialization and deserialization.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate notices the serialVersionUID warning and understands why exceptions have it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Throwable implements Serializable, wondering why the IDE warns about serialVersionUID in exception classes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the serialization version contract and when it actually matters for exceptions

sections.title: Why Exceptions Need serialVersionUID
sections.content:
**Throwable** implements `java.io.Serializable`. This means all exceptions are serializable by default. When Java serializes an object, it includes a version identifier. If the class has changed when you try to deserialize, Java needs to verify compatibility using `serialVersionUID`.

For most application exceptions, serialization isn't actually used — exceptions aren't sent over the wire directly. However:
- Without a declared serialVersionUID, Java generates one based on class structure
- If you change the class (add a field), the generated ID changes → deserialization fails
- Declaring `private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;` pins the version

IDEs warn about missing serialVersionUID for any Serializable class, including exceptions.

sections.title: Declaring serialVersionUID
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Throwable implements Serializable, which means all exception classes are serializable by default. That's why your IDE warns you to add serialVersionUID to your custom exception — it's any serializable class warning. The serialVersionUID is used to verify that the class version during deserialization matches the version during serialization. In practice, for application exceptions, you're not usually serializing and sending them over a wire, so it's more of a best practice declaration. You just add private static final long serialVersionUID equals 1L and the warning goes away. If you ever change the class significantly in a way that breaks deserialization compatibility, you'd bump it to 2L.
